questions.stem: The 1949 armistice agreements that ended the first Arab-Israeli war:
options: created an independent Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza alongside Israel
returned all Palestinian refugees to their homes under United Nations supervision
gave Jerusalem to international control under the terms of the 1947 partition plan
set ceasefire lines, later called the Green Line, but no peace treaties
questions.explanation: Israel signed armistices with Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria in 1949. Israel held more land than the UN plan had proposed; Jordan held the West Bank and East Jerusalem and Egypt held Gaza. No Arab state recognised Israel.

questions.stem: UN General Assembly Resolution 194 (December 1948) is often cited in debates over Palestinian refugees because it said that:
options: refugees would lose any claim to property if they did not return within one year
refugees wishing to return and live in peace should be allowed to, or be compensated
all refugees must be resettled permanently in the Arab countries where they had fled
Israel must accept the 1947 partition borders before any refugee could return home
questions.explanation: Palestinians and Arab states see Resolution 194 as the basis of a 'right of return'. Israel has argued that a large return would end its Jewish majority. The issue remains one of the hardest in any peace settlement.

questions.stem: UNRWA, set up by the United Nations in 1949, was created to:
options: settle Jewish refugees from Europe and Arab countries in Israel
provide relief, schooling and health care to Palestinian refugees
keep the peace along the Israeli-Egyptian armistice line in the Sinai
oversee the division of Jerusalem between Israel and Jordan
questions.explanation: The UN Relief and Works Agency still runs schools, clinics and camps for registered Palestinian refugees and their descendants in Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, the West Bank and Gaza. Its long existence reflects the failure to resolve the refugee issue.

questions.stem: In the years after 1948, hundreds of thousands of Jews left or were forced out of Arab countries such as Iraq, Yemen and Egypt. For a study of the conflict, this is significant because:
options: these migrants mostly moved to Europe rather than Israel, weakening the new state
it was organised by the Arab League to strengthen Arab claims to Palestine
it added a second refugee story that Israelis set beside the Palestinian refugee issue
it ended the conflict by giving Israel enough population to make peace with its neighbours
questions.explanation: Most of these Jews settled in Israel, changing its society. Israeli governments have argued their losses should be considered alongside Palestinian claims, while critics say the two cases are different. It shows how competing narratives of loss shape the conflict.

questions.stem: In July 1956 Egypt's President Nasser nationalised:
options: the Sinai railways
the Suez Canal Company
the Aswan High Dam
the Egyptian oil fields
questions.explanation: Nasser took over the British and French-owned company after the USA and Britain withdrew funding for the Aswan Dam. Canal tolls were to pay for the dam instead.

questions.stem: In October-November 1956 Israel, Britain and France attacked Egypt after a secret agreement. How did the Suez Crisis end?
options: Britain and France kept the canal zone and returned it to Egypt only in 1967
Egypt surrendered the canal and recognised Israel in a treaty signed in London
Israel annexed the Sinai Peninsula with the agreement of the United Nations
US and Soviet pressure forced a withdrawal, and a UN force went to Sinai
questions.explanation: Eisenhower opposed the invasion and used financial pressure on Britain. The first armed UN peacekeeping force, UNEF, was sent to the Egypt-Israel border. Nasser emerged as a hero of Arab nationalism despite military defeat.

questions.stem: Australia's Prime Minister Robert Menzies played a part in the Suez Crisis by:
options: leading a mission to Cairo urging Nasser to accept international control of the canal
sending Australian troops to join the British and French landings at Port Said in November 1956
chairing the UN General Assembly session that condemned Israel, Britain and France
proposing the UN peacekeeping force that was later sent to separate Egypt and Israel
questions.explanation: In September 1956 Menzies headed a five-nation committee that presented Nasser with a plan for international management of the canal, which he rejected. Australia supported Britain diplomatically but did not send forces. Canada's Lester Pearson proposed UNEF.

questions.stem: The Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) was founded in 1964 with the support of:
options: the Arab League
the United Nations
the Soviet Union
the State of Israel
questions.explanation: The PLO was created at an Arab League summit, initially under Egyptian influence. After 1967 guerrilla groups, above all Yasser Arafat's Fatah, took control, and Arafat became chairman in 1969.

questions.stem: Which events of May 1967 led directly to the Six-Day War?
options: The United States announced it would stop all military aid to Israel
Nasser had UN peacekeepers leave Sinai and closed the Straits of Tiran to Israel
Israel annexed East Jerusalem and began building settlements in the West Bank
Jordan's King Hussein expelled the PLO, which then attacked Israel from Lebanon
questions.explanation: Egypt moved troops into Sinai, UNEF withdrew at Nasser's request, and closing the straits cut Israel's route to Eilat, which Israel had declared a cause for war. Israel launched a pre-emptive strike on 5 June 1967.

questions.stem: In the Six-Day War of June 1967, Israel captured:
options: the West Bank only, after Jordan alone attacked Israel
Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights
Sinai and the Suez Canal zone only, which it returned within a month
southern Lebanon and the city of Damascus, the capital of Syria
questions.explanation: The rapid victory tripled the territory under Israeli control and brought around a million Palestinians under military occupation. The fate of these territories has been at the centre of every peace effort since.

questions.stem: UN Security Council Resolution 242 (November 1967) called for Israel's withdrawal 'from territories occupied in the recent conflict' and for every state's right to live in peace within secure borders. Why has its wording been debated?
options: The English text omits 'the' before 'territories', so Israel said full withdrawal was not required
It named the Palestine Liberation Organization as the government of the occupied territories
It required Israel to return to the 1947 partition borders rather than the 1949 armistice lines
It was passed by the General Assembly, so most states argued it had no legal force at all
questions.explanation: Resolution 242 set out the formula of 'land for peace' but left the extent of withdrawal unclear. It referred to a just settlement of 'the refugee problem' without naming Palestinians as a nation, which the PLO at first rejected.

questions.stem: At the Khartoum summit of September 1967, Arab leaders adopted a position often summarised as the 'three nos'. These were:
options: no peace with, no recognition of and no negotiations with Israel
no oil for the West, no Soviet bases and no American aid to Arab states
no Palestinian state, no refugee return and no division of Jerusalem
no war with Israel, no support for the PLO and no closure of the canal
questions.explanation: The Khartoum Resolution reflected anger after defeat and made early peace talks unlikely. Israel cited it as evidence that land-for-peace had no Arab partner, though Egypt and Jordan quietly explored diplomacy afterwards.

questions.stem: In September 1970, known to Palestinians as 'Black September', King Hussein of Jordan:
options: signed a peace treaty with Israel and handed the West Bank to Palestinian rule
joined Egypt in a surprise attack on Israel to recover the West Bank
made Yasser Arafat prime minister of Jordan to end the civil conflict
drove armed Palestinian groups out of Jordan, and many moved to Lebanon
questions.explanation: PLO groups had become a state within a state in Jordan and had hijacked airliners. After heavy fighting, the PLO relocated to Lebanon, which helped destabilise that country. Jordan's peace treaty with Israel came only in 1994.

questions.stem: The October War of 1973, known in Israel as the Yom Kippur War, began when:
options: Israel invaded Egypt to destroy Soviet missiles being built near the Suez Canal
Jordan and Iraq attacked Israel to recover the West Bank and East Jerusalem
the PLO seized the Golan Heights from Israel with Syrian help
Egypt and Syria made a surprise attack on the holiest day of the Jewish year
questions.explanation: Egyptian forces crossed the Suez Canal and Syria attacked on the Golan on 6 October 1973. Israel recovered after early losses, helped by a US airlift. Egypt's early success restored Arab pride and made later negotiation politically possible for Sadat.

questions.stem: During the 1973 war, Arab oil producers cut production and embargoed the United States and the Netherlands. The main result was that:
options: Israel withdrew from all the territory it had captured in 1967 within a year
the embargo collapsed within days because Europe had large oil reserves
oil prices rose sharply and Western states took Arab concerns more seriously
the United States stopped supplying weapons to Israel for the rest of the decade
questions.explanation: The price of oil roughly quadrupled, causing economic shock in the West. The embargo showed the political power of oil and encouraged US diplomatic engagement, including Henry Kissinger's shuttle diplomacy.

questions.stem: Henry Kissinger's 'shuttle diplomacy' after the 1973 war achieved:
options: the return of the Golan Heights to Syria in exchange for recognition
agreements separating Israeli forces from the Egyptian and Syrian armies
a comprehensive peace treaty between Israel and all its Arab neighbours
the recognition of the PLO by the United States and Israel in 1974
questions.explanation: Flying between capitals, Kissinger negotiated step-by-step agreements in 1974-75. They reduced the risk of renewed war and drew Egypt towards the United States, preparing the ground for later peace.

questions.stem: In 1974 the Arab League recognised the PLO as the 'sole legitimate representative' of the Palestinian people, and Yasser Arafat addressed the UN General Assembly. This was significant because it:
options: established the PLO internationally as the voice of Palestinian aims
ended the PLO's armed struggle and committed it to recognise Israel
made Jordan the official representative of Palestinians at the UN
led Israel to open direct negotiations with the PLO that same year
questions.explanation: The PLO gained observer status at the UN, and Palestinians were increasingly seen as a people with national rights rather than only as refugees. Israel refused to deal with the PLO until 1993.

questions.stem: In November 1977 Egypt's President Anwar Sadat:
options: recognised the PLO as the government of Egypt's Sinai Peninsula
announced that Egypt would leave the Arab League and join NATO
travelled to Jerusalem and addressed the Israeli parliament, the Knesset
expelled all Soviet advisers and declared war on Israel for the third time
questions.explanation: Sadat's visit was the first by an Arab head of state to Israel and broke a powerful taboo. He hoped to recover Sinai and ease Egypt's economic burden of war. Many Arab governments condemned the visit.

questions.stem: The Camp David Accords of September 1978, brokered by President Carter between Sadat and Israel's Prime Minister Menachem Begin, led to:
options: a joint Arab-Israeli government for Jerusalem under United Nations supervision
the immediate return of the Golan Heights to Syria and of the West Bank to Jordan
an Egypt-Israel peace treaty in 1979 under which Israel returned Sinai
a Palestinian state in Gaza and the West Bank declared in the same year
questions.explanation: Egypt became the first Arab state to recognise Israel, and Sinai was returned by 1982. A second framework on Palestinian autonomy was never put into effect. Sadat and Begin shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the Egypt-Israel peace of 1979?
options: It created a Palestinian state, though the borders of the state were disputed
It ended war between the two states but did not resolve the Palestinian question
It ended the Arab-Israeli conflict, since all other Arab states soon followed Egypt
It failed within two years, as war resumed between Egypt and Israel in 1981
questions.explanation: The 'cold peace' has lasted, removing the largest Arab army from the conflict. But Egypt was suspended from the Arab League, Sadat was assassinated by Islamist officers in 1981, and the Palestinian autonomy talks went nowhere.

questions.stem: Israel invaded Lebanon in June 1982 mainly to:
options: seize Lebanese oil fields to replace oil lost when Sinai was returned
rescue Israeli hostages held by Hezbollah in the city of Beirut
destroy the PLO's base there and stop attacks on northern Israel
protect Lebanon's government from a Syrian invasion requested by the UN
questions.explanation: Israeli forces reached Beirut, and the PLO leadership and fighters were evacuated, with Arafat moving to Tunis. Israel occupied a zone in southern Lebanon until 2000, during which Hezbollah emerged as its main opponent.

questions.stem: In September 1982, Lebanese Christian Phalangist militia killed hundreds of Palestinian and Lebanese civilians in the Sabra and Shatila camps in Beirut, in an area under Israeli army control. Israel's Kahan Commission later:
options: found that Israeli soldiers had carried out the killings on Begin's direct orders
cleared all Israeli officials and blamed the PLO for the deaths in the camps
recommended that Israel withdraw from Lebanon within one week of its report
found Defence Minister Ariel Sharon indirectly responsible, and he left the post
questions.explanation: The inquiry found Israeli leaders had failed to prevent the massacre despite foreseeable danger. The killings caused protests in Israel and worldwide. Sharon later became prime minister in 2001.

questions.stem: The First Intifada, which began in December 1987, was:
options: a war between Israel and Syria for control of the Golan Heights and Lebanon
an Israeli military campaign to expel the PLO from its base in Tunisia
a revolt by Lebanese Shia militias against the Palestinian refugee camps
a mass Palestinian uprising in the West Bank and Gaza against occupation
questions.explanation: It began in Gaza and spread, involving strikes, boycotts and stone-throwing youths, coordinated largely by local leaders rather than the exiled PLO. Images of Israeli soldiers confronting young protesters affected world opinion.

questions.stem: Hamas, founded in Gaza in 1987 during the First Intifada, differed from the PLO's Fatah mainly because it:
options: was an Islamist movement that rejected recognising Israel
was a secular movement committed to negotiating with Israel
was a Christian militia based in Lebanon allied to Israel
was set up by Egypt to govern Gaza on its behalf after 1967
questions.explanation: Hamas grew from the Muslim Brotherhood and combined social services with armed struggle. It opposed the Oslo process and carried out suicide bombings in the 1990s and 2000s. Fatah was secular nationalist and came to accept negotiation.

questions.stem: In late 1988 the PLO declared a State of Palestine, and Arafat accepted Resolution 242 and renounced terrorism. Why was this a turning point?
options: It united the PLO and Hamas in a single government under Arafat's leadership
It implied recognising Israel and opened the way to US talks with the PLO
It ended the First Intifada immediately and led to Israeli withdrawal from Gaza
It was accepted by Israel, which recognised the State of Palestine that year
questions.explanation: Accepting 242 meant accepting a state alongside Israel, a major shift from the goal of liberating all of Palestine. The USA began a dialogue with the PLO. Jordan had given up its claims to the West Bank earlier in 1988.

questions.stem: The Oslo Accords, signed at the White House in September 1993, began with:
options: mutual recognition by Israel and the PLO and a plan for Palestinian self-rule
a full peace treaty creating an independent Palestinian state with set borders
Israel's agreement to return to the 1967 lines and divide Jerusalem at once
the PLO's agreement to dissolve itself and accept Jordanian rule of the West Bank
questions.explanation: Secret talks in Norway produced the Declaration of Principles, symbolised by the handshake of Yitzhak Rabin and Yasser Arafat. A Palestinian Authority was set up in 1994. Rabin, Shimon Peres and Arafat shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize.

questions.stem: The Oslo process left the hardest issues to 'final status' talks. Which issues were they?
options: the Suez Canal, Sinai oil and Nile water rights
Lebanon's civil war and Syria's role in Beirut
Iran's nuclear program and sanctions on Iraq
Jerusalem, refugees, settlements and borders
questions.explanation: Interim agreements were meant to build trust before these core questions were settled within five years. Critics argue that postponing them allowed settlement growth and violence to undermine the process.

questions.stem: In 1994, building on the momentum of Oslo, Israel signed a peace treaty with:
options: Syria
Lebanon
Iraq
Jordan
questions.explanation: King Hussein and Prime Minister Rabin signed the treaty in October 1994, making Jordan the second Arab state, after Egypt, to make peace with Israel. Talks with Syria over the Golan Heights failed.

questions.stem: Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated in Tel Aviv in November 1995 by:
options: a Hamas gunman who had crossed into Israel from the Gaza Strip
a Syrian agent seeking to stop negotiations over the Golan Heights
a PLO member who rejected Arafat's leadership and the Oslo deal
an Israeli extremist who opposed giving land to the Palestinians
questions.explanation: Yigal Amir killed Rabin after a peace rally. The assassination deepened divisions in Israel, and in 1996 Benjamin Netanyahu, a critic of Oslo, won the election. Many historians see it as a major blow to the peace process.

questions.stem: Edward Said, the Palestinian-American scholar, criticised the Oslo Accords from the start mainly because he believed they:
options: were negotiated by the United Nations without any Palestinian participation
gave up too much without guaranteeing a Palestinian state or an end to occupation
forced Israel to withdraw too quickly from the whole of the West Bank and Gaza
ignored Jordan's rightful claim to govern the West Bank on behalf of Palestinians
questions.explanation: Said argued the PLO had recognised Israel and accepted limited autonomy while key issues such as settlements and refugees were left open. Israeli critics on the right argued the opposite, that Oslo gave too much to the PLO.

questions.stem: Historians and participants disagree about why the Camp David summit of July 2000 failed. Robert Malley and Hussein Agha challenged the view that Arafat alone was to blame by arguing that:
options: the summit never discussed Jerusalem or refugees, so failure was certain from the start
Israel's prime minister Ehud Barak refused to attend and sent junior officials
all sides erred, and Israel's offer fell short of what Palestinians could accept
Arafat had accepted every Israeli proposal, but the United States vetoed the deal
questions.explanation: US negotiator Dennis Ross and Barak blamed Arafat for rejecting a generous offer without a counter-proposal. Malley, a US official at the summit, and Agha argued the offer was not as generous as claimed and the process was badly handled by all.

questions.stem: The Second Intifada, which broke out in September 2000, differed from the first mainly in:
options: its location in southern Lebanon rather than in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip
its quick end within a month after the Camp David summit succeeded
its greater use of armed attacks, including suicide bombings, and heavier Israeli force
its reliance on nonviolent boycotts and strikes led by the local Palestinian leadership
questions.explanation: It followed Ariel Sharon's visit to the Temple Mount (Haram al-Sharif) and the failure of Camp David. Far more people were killed than in the first intifada, and Israel began building a separation barrier in the West Bank from 2002.

questions.stem: In 2005 Israel withdrew its settlers and soldiers from Gaza. In 2006-07:
options: Fatah and Hamas formed a united government that negotiated a final peace
Egypt annexed Gaza with the agreement of Israel and the United Nations
Israel reoccupied Gaza permanently and rebuilt the settlements
Hamas won Palestinian elections and then took control of Gaza from Fatah
questions.explanation: Hamas won the January 2006 legislative elections, and after fighting with Fatah seized Gaza in June 2007. Israel and Egypt imposed a blockade, and the split between a Hamas-run Gaza and a Fatah-led West Bank complicated negotiations.

questions.stem: The Arab Peace Initiative of 2002, proposed by Saudi Arabia and endorsed by the Arab League, offered:
options: the resettlement of all Palestinian refugees in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf states
normal relations with Israel for withdrawal to 1967 lines and a Palestinian state
Arab recognition of Israel's annexation of the West Bank in exchange for oil agreements
a joint Arab military alliance with Israel against Iran without any Palestinian state
questions.explanation: The initiative also called for a just solution to the refugee issue. Israel did not accept its terms, but it marked a change from the 'three nos' of 1967 towards collective Arab acceptance of Israel in principle.

questions.stem: The Abraham Accords of 2020 are significant because:
options: Israel and the Palestinian Authority signed a final status agreement creating two states
Egypt and Jordan ended their peace treaties with Israel in protest at settlement growth
Iran and Israel agreed to end their rivalry and open embassies in each other's capitals
the UAE and Bahrain normalised ties with Israel without a Palestinian deal first
questions.explanation: Brokered by the United States, the accords were followed by agreements with Sudan and Morocco. They broke with the Arab Peace Initiative's sequence of peace with Palestinians first, which Palestinian leaders condemned.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the view that peace in the Middle East since 1948 has come mainly through agreements between states rather than a settlement of the Palestinian question?
options: Palestinians held elections for a legislative council in 1996 and again in 2006
Egypt (1979) and Jordan (1994) made lasting treaties with Israel, but Oslo's final talks failed
The PLO was recognised by the Arab League in 1974 as the sole representative of the Palestinians
UN Resolution 242 set out the principle of land for peace after the Six-Day War
questions.explanation: State-to-state treaties have endured, and the Abraham Accords followed the same pattern, but the core Israeli-Palestinian issues remain unresolved. The other options describe Palestinian representation or principles rather than comparing outcomes.
